artwork.title: Borghese Gladiator
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Jastrow, 2006, via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

lessons.title: A warrior without his weapons

n1.text: A nude marble fighter lunges forward. His weight is on his bent right leg, and his left arm is flung up high.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Follow one line from his back foot to his raised fist. Then look where his eyes are turned.

q1.text: Despite his famous name, what is he?

b1a.text: The name is old, but it is wrong.

correction.tempting: It is the statue's famous name.
correction.truth: He is a warrior in battle. A shield once hung on his raised left arm.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

b1b.text: Yes. The Louvre calls him a fighting warrior. His left arm carried a shield, and his right hand probably held a sword. Both are lost.

b1c.text: Nothing was thrown: he was fighting.

correction.tempting: His arm is flung out like a thrower's.
correction.truth: His left arm carried a shield and his right hand probably a sword. Both are lost.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

n2.text: Beside his right leg stands a carved tree trunk. On it, the sculptor cut a signature in Greek letters.

q2.text: What does the signature tell us, besides the sculptor's name?

b2a.text: No date: the signature names a family and a city.

correction.tempting: Signatures today often carry a date.
correction.truth: It reads: Agasias, son of Dositheos, of Ephesus, made it.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

correction.tempting: Many ancient works name the person who paid.
correction.truth: It names only the sculptor, his father and his city: Agasias, son of Dositheos, of Ephesus.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica.

b2c.text: Yes. It reads: Agasias, son of Dositheos, of Ephesus, made it.

n7.text: Now the stone. Scientists can tell one white marble from another, and trace a statue's block to the mountain it came from.

q5.text: So where was this fighter's marble quarried?

b5a.text: Yes. The Louvre records Pentelic marble, from Mount Pentelicus near Athens: the marble of the Parthenon frieze. A sculptor from Ephesus, Athenian stone, found in Italy.

correction.tempting: He was dug up in Italy.
correction.truth: His marble is Pentelic, from Mount Pentelicus near Athens: the marble of the Parthenon frieze.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record and Greece teaching file; Roworth, Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009); University of Georgia (2001).

b5c.text: Not from Ephesus: from near Athens.

correction.truth: His marble is Pentelic, from Mount Pentelicus near Athens: the marble of the Parthenon frieze.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record and Greece teaching file; Roworth, Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009); University of Georgia (2001).

n3.text: The Louvre catalogues it as a Hellenistic work by Agasias, made about 100 BC. Not everyone agrees.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: A name on a statue sounds like the end of the story. Here, it is where the arguing starts.

q3.text: Is it Agasias's own design, or a copy of an older statue?

b3a.text: That is one view, not a settled fact.

correction.tempting: He signed it, so it must be his.
correction.truth: Some scholars think Agasias copied an older bronze; a 2009 study calls the statue a Roman copy.
correction.evidence: Treccani's Enciclopedia dell'Arte Antica; Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009).

b3b.text: That is one view, not a settled fact.

correction.tempting: Many marble statues in Rome are copies.
correction.truth: The Louvre catalogues it as Agasias's Hellenistic work of about 100 BC; others disagree.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009).

b3c.text: Yes. The Louvre treats it as Agasias's work of about 100 BC. Others have thought he copied an older bronze, or that this is a later Roman copy.

n4.text: It was found near Anzio, in Italy, and joined the collection of Cardinal Scipione Borghese in Rome. That is how it got its name.

q4.text: How did the statue come to Paris?

choices.label: A pope gave it to France

correction.tempting: It left a Roman collection for Paris.
correction.truth: Prince Camillo Borghese sold it to the Louvre in 1807.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009).

b4b.text: Yes. Prince Camillo Borghese sold it to the Louvre in 1807, and by 1811 it was on show in Paris.

b4c.text: No pope gave it away: a Borghese prince sold it.

correction.tempting: It was found in Papal Rome and kept by a cardinal.
correction.truth: Prince Camillo Borghese sold it to the Louvre in 1807.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Metropolitan Museum Journal (2009).

n5.text: Artists borrowed his pose for generations. Painters echoed it, and students drew small copies of him by lamplight.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Picture students sketching a small copy of him by lamplight. Which line of his body would you draw first?

n6.text: A warrior without his weapons, under a name that does not fit. He stands in Room 348, on Floor 0 of the Sully wing.

lessons.takeaway: A marble warrior, not a gladiator, signed in Greek by Agasias of Ephesus and carved in Pentelic marble from near Athens: scholars still argue whether he made it or copied an older statue, and the Louvre bought it in 1807.
